items.prompt: Why can algae survive perfectly well in water without ever growing roots?

options.label: It gets everything it needs delivered by ocean currents to a fixed feeding point
options.feedback: Algae has no single feeding point that currents deliver to; nutrients are taken in across its whole body, not at one spot.

options.label: It absorbs water and nutrients directly through its entire surface
options.feedback: With every cell already sitting in water carrying dissolved minerals, an alga absorbs what it needs directly across its own surface.

options.label: It draws nutrients up from the seafloor through its base
options.feedback: Many algae never touch the seafloor at all, drifting freely in open water, so nutrients cannot be arriving through a base pressed into the ground.

options.label: It stores enough nutrients before birth to last its whole life
options.feedback: No alga is born with a lifetime supply already stored; it has to keep taking in nutrients continuously as it grows.

items.ok_line: Surrounded by water, so every surface can absorb.
items.ko_line: Every part of the alga is already in contact with the water it needs.
items.exp_title: A body already surrounded by everything it needs
items.exp_text: Because an alga is either fully submerged or constantly wet, every cell on its surface sits in direct contact with water carrying dissolved minerals, and those cells simply absorb what they need straight across their outer membrane. With water and nutrients available at every point of its body at once, an alga has no need for the specialized underground network a land plant relies on to search for them.

items.prompt: How does giant kelp keep its long blades floating up near the sunlit surface of the water?

options.label: It grows only in water shallow enough that the surface is always close
options.feedback: Giant kelp grows in water far deeper than its own height would let it simply touch the surface; something else has to lift its blades upward.

options.label: Its blades are naturally lighter than water
options.feedback: Kelp tissue on its own is not especially light; without help it would sink rather than rise toward the surface.

options.label: Currents constantly push it upward from below
options.feedback: Currents move kelp sideways more than they lift it; nothing about a current would reliably hold blades near the surface.

options.label: Small gas-filled bladders along its stalk give it buoyancy
options.feedback: Small gas-filled bladders along the stalk provide the lift that holds the blade upright toward the sunlit water above.

items.ok_line: Gas pockets doing exactly what a life jacket does.
items.ko_line: The kelp is carrying its own built-in flotation devices.
items.exp_text: At the base of each blade, giant kelp grows a small round bladder filled with gas, and the combined lift from many of these bladders along a single stalk is enough to hold the whole long blade upright toward the sunlit water above. Without that lift, the same blade would simply lie flat against the seafloor, folded in on itself and shaded from the light it needs to grow.

items.prompt: What is the actual job of the root-like structure a kelp uses to attach itself to a rock?

options.label: It anchors the kelp firmly without absorbing any nutrients
options.feedback: The holdfast grips the rock tightly enough to keep the kelp from being torn away, without absorbing anything itself.

options.label: It absorbs water and minerals the same way a plant root does
options.feedback: This structure takes in nothing from the rock; all of the kelp's absorbing happens elsewhere, across its blades.

options.label: It slowly dissolves the rock to extract minerals
options.feedback: It has no role in dissolving or extracting anything from the rock; its only job is to hold on.

options.label: It grows deep cracks into the rock to store food
options.feedback: There is no storage happening inside the rock; the structure exists purely to keep the kelp from being swept away.

items.ok_line: It holds the kelp in place and does nothing else.
items.ko_line: This structure looks like a root but does not do a root's other jobs.
items.exp_text: The branching, root-shaped structure at the base of a kelp, called a holdfast, grips tightly onto a rock or other hard surface purely to keep the kelp from being torn away by waves and currents. Unlike a plant's root, it draws in no water and no nutrients at all, since the entire rest of the kelp already absorbs everything it needs directly through its blades in the surrounding water.

items.prompt: Why is a diatom's glassy shell often compared to a small pillbox?

options.label: It is a single solid case that the diatom seals itself inside
options.feedback: The shell is not one sealed case; it is built from two separate pieces, which is exactly what makes the pillbox comparison apt in the first place.

options.label: It is soft and flexible enough to open like a hinged lid
options.feedback: The shell is rigid, made of glass-like silica, and does not flex open on a hinge the way a soft container might.

options.label: It is made of two overlapping halves that fit together like a lid and base
options.feedback: The larger of the two silica valves overlaps the smaller one, the way a lid overlaps the base of a small box.

options.label: It changes shape completely as the diatom grows larger
options.feedback: The shell itself is rigid and does not reshape as the diatom grows; growth is handled by other means, not by the shell changing form.

items.ok_line: Two rigid halves, one fitting neatly over the other.
items.ko_line: The comparison to a pillbox comes from how the shell is built out of two overlapping pieces.
items.exp_title: Two glassy halves, one over the other
items.exp_text: A diatom builds its shell out of silica, the same hard mineral found in glass and sand, forming two slightly different-sized halves called valves that fit together with the larger one overlapping the smaller like the lid of a small box overlapping its base. When the diatom eventually divides, each half keeps one of the original valves and grows a new, smaller one to complete the pair, which is why diatom populations tend to shrink in average size over many generations.

items.prompt: How do the countless tiny algae drifting near the ocean's surface end up supplying so much of the oxygen in the air?

options.label: A few unusually large algae species produce most of it
options.feedback: The oxygen is not coming from a handful of especially large species; it comes from the sheer number of ordinary, tiny algae photosynthesizing at once.

options.label: Enormous numbers of them photosynthesize across the entire sunlit ocean surface
options.feedback: Countless tiny cells across the entire sunlit ocean surface each photosynthesize a little, and combined they add up to a substantial share of the world's oxygen.

options.label: They release oxygen stored from deep water they once drifted through
options.feedback: Algae are not releasing a stored reserve gathered from deeper water; the oxygen they give off is produced fresh, through photosynthesis, in the sunlit layer where they live.

options.label: Ocean currents concentrate oxygen that algae originally trapped near shore
options.feedback: Currents do not gather and concentrate oxygen this way; the oxygen enters the air directly from wherever each alga happens to be photosynthesizing.

items.ok_line: Not one giant producer — countless tiny ones, everywhere at once.
items.ko_line: The real explanation is simply how much surface area is covered by these tiny organisms.
items.exp_title: A vast number of small producers
items.exp_text: Each single-celled alga photosynthesizes on a tiny scale, releasing only a faint trace of oxygen as it converts sunlight and carbon dioxide into sugar. But the sunlit layer of the ocean covers most of the planet's surface and is filled with these cells in staggering numbers, so their combined, simultaneous photosynthesis is what actually supplies that oxygen, cell by tiny cell.

items.prompt: Why can red algae grow in deeper water than green algae typically can?

options.label: Red algae do not need light to photosynthesize at all
options.feedback: Red algae still need light for photosynthesis just as green algae do; the difference is which part of the light they can use, not whether light matters.

options.label: Red algae grow much more slowly, so they need less energy
options.feedback: Slower growth would not by itself let an alga reach deeper water; the real difference lies in what wavelengths of light it can actually absorb and use.

options.label: Red algae feed on nutrients that only exist at greater depths
options.feedback: The nutrients red algae use are not unique to deep water; the limitation on depth comes from light, not from where particular nutrients are found.

options.label: Red algae contain pigments that absorb the blue-green light reaching those depths
options.feedback: Red algae's pigments are tuned to absorb the blue-green light that survives being filtered by the water above.

items.ok_line: Catching the light that's actually left down there.
items.ko_title: It comes down to which light gets used
items.ko_line: Depth changes which colors of light are still available — and that is what the difference in pigment is suited to.
items.exp_title: Tuned to the light that survives the depth
items.exp_text: As sunlight passes down through water, red and orange wavelengths are absorbed first, near the surface, leaving mostly blue-green light to reach greater depths. Red algae carry pigments built to capture exactly that blue-green light and pass its energy on for photosynthesis, letting them keep making food in dim water where green algae's pigments, tuned to different wavelengths, can no longer find enough light to use.

items.prompt: What causes a pond's surface to suddenly turn thick green within just a few days?

options.label: A surge of nutrients lets algae cells divide rapidly
options.feedback: A sudden surge of nutrients lets algae divide again and again, turning a small population into a visible bloom within days.

options.label: Fish in the pond release a pigment that colors the water
options.feedback: Fish are not producing the pigment responsible for the color; the green comes from the algae itself multiplying in the water.

options.label: Sunlight changes the color of the water directly
options.feedback: Sunlight alone does not turn water green; it is the buildup of countless algae cells reflecting green light that produces the color.

options.label: Wind blows algae in from a nearby pond
options.feedback: The bloom is not usually blown in from elsewhere; it grows from algae already present in the pond, multiplying rapidly in place.

items.ok_line: Extra nutrients, and the algae take full advantage.
items.ko_line: The green comes from a sudden increase in the number of algae cells already living in the water.
items.exp_title: A population that doubles and doubles again
items.exp_text: When fertilizer runoff or other nutrients flood into a pond, the algae already living there suddenly have far more of what they need to grow, and each cell can divide into two in only a short span before dividing again. Repeated doubling this way turns a modest, invisible population into a dense green layer covering the entire surface, simply because the growth compounds so quickly once it starts.

items.prompt: How can a thick mat of algae covering a pond end up killing the fish living beneath it?

options.label: The algae release a poison that spreads through the water
options.feedback: Poison release is not the general mechanism here; the harm comes from a chain of effects on light and oxygen, not from a toxin being spread.

options.label: The mat traps heat and cooks the water below it
options.feedback: A surface mat does not trap enough heat to raise the water's temperature dangerously; the real danger works through light and oxygen, not warmth.

options.label: It blocks sunlight from underwater plants, which then die and use up oxygen as they decompose
options.feedback: Blocking sunlight kills the underwater plants, and their decomposition then consumes the oxygen the fish depend on.

options.label: It absorbs so much water that the pond simply dries up
options.feedback: Algae do not draw enough water out of a pond to dry it up; the danger to the fish comes from a change in the water's oxygen, not its water level.

items.ok_line: Blocked light leads to dead plants, and dead plants steal the oxygen.
items.ko_line: Follow what happens to the plants underneath the mat, and then to their remains.
items.exp_title: A chain that ends in suffocation
items.exp_text: A thick mat of algae covering the surface blocks sunlight from reaching the underwater plants below, and without light those plants can no longer photosynthesize and soon die. Bacteria then set to work decomposing all that dead plant material, and their own activity consumes large amounts of dissolved oxygen from the water, leaving too little behind for the fish that depend on it to breathe.

items.prompt: How do most algae manage to multiply into such enormous numbers so quickly?

options.label: They lay eggs that hatch within hours
options.feedback: Algae do not reproduce by laying eggs; their multiplication happens through a much simpler process at the level of a single cell.

options.label: Each cell simply divides in two, over and over
options.feedback: A single cell alone is enough to produce two new cells, with no need for eggs, seeds, or a partner.

options.label: They release seeds that scatter across the water
options.feedback: Algae produce no seeds; that is a structure belonging to a completely different kind of organism, not to algae.

options.label: Pairs of algae combine to form several new cells at once
options.feedback: Ordinary algal multiplication does not depend on pairs combining; a single cell alone is enough to produce two new cells.

items.ok_line: One cell becomes two, and two become four.
items.ko_title: No eggs, no seeds, no pairing needed
items.ko_line: A single algal cell is enough, all on its own, to make more of itself.
items.exp_title: Doubling, one cell at a time
items.exp_text: A single algal cell reproduces simply by growing to roughly twice its normal size and then splitting cleanly into two complete, independent cells, each capable of repeating the process again almost immediately. Because this doubling needs no partner and no waiting for eggs or seeds to develop, a population that starts as a handful of cells can swell into a visible bloom within a stretch of favorable weather.

items.prompt: Why do some algae grow as long chains of cells instead of drifting as separate individual cells?

options.label: Chains form when a predator glues surviving cells together
options.feedback: No predator is responsible for linking the cells; the chain forms from the alga's own way of dividing, not from an outside attack.

options.label: Each cell in the chain is actually a different species growing together
options.feedback: A chain like this is made of identical cells belonging to the same alga, not several different species joined together.

options.label: Currents tangle free-floating cells into chain-like clumps
options.feedback: The chain is not a tangle caused by water movement; the cells are directly connected to each other from the moment they are produced.

options.label: Daughter cells stay attached to each other after dividing
options.feedback: The daughter cells produced by division stay joined at their shared wall instead of separating, building an unbroken chain.

items.ok_line: Division without separation is what builds the chain.
items.ko_title: Not predators, mixed species, or tangling
items.ko_line: The chain comes from how the cells are produced in the first place, not from anything happening to them afterward.
items.exp_title: A chain built by staying attached
items.exp_text: When a single algal cell divides, the two resulting daughter cells in some species remain joined at their shared wall rather than drifting apart, and each of those cells later divides again while still attached to the last. Repeating this over many divisions produces a long, unbroken filament made of identical cells lined up end to end, all descended from the very same original cell.
